# What is {workr}?

A **very** simple R data pipeline

::: {.notes}
~0:00–4:00. One sentence: workr runs YAML-defined pipelines of R function
calls. Everything else builds on that.
:::

## Workflows are YAML files <above>easily parsed to an R `list`</above>

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="|2-4|5-14"}
# hello_cars.yaml
meta:
  ID: hello_cars
  col: speed
steps:
  - name: dplyr::pull
    output: speed
    params:
      df: df
      col: col
  - name: mean
    output: result
    params:
      lData: speed
```

::: {.notes}
`meta` = metadata (highlighted first). `steps` = ordered function calls
(highlighted second). Each step names a function, its `output`, and its
`params`. `meta` values can be referenced by steps.
:::

## `workr::RunWorkflow()`

### Inputs
- workflow (YAML parsed to a `list`)
- initial data (`lData`) — available to every step, updated as steps run

### Output
- Returns the result of the last step by default
- `bReturnResult = FALSE` returns the full workflow object with all
  intermediate outputs

::: {.notes}
`RunWorkflows()` (plural) chains multiple workflows, feeding each output into
the next `lData`.
:::

## That's really about it

- Minimal mental model
- Easy to read / debug
- Surprisingly scalable

# Why {workr}?

Scalable clinical-trial operations

::: {.notes}
~4:00–8:00. The origin story: this came out of a real scale problem, not an
academic exercise.
:::

## From safety monitoring to risk-based quality monitoring

- `{gsm}` (Good Statistical Monitoring) is a qualified set of R packages
  providing a GxP framework for central monitoring in clinical trials
- Repeatability and scale are the whole game:
  - 30 studies × monthly snapshots × 15 metrics × 5 steps
  - **~27,000 metrics / year**

::: {.notes}
The number is the point — hand-written per-study scripts do not survive this.
:::

## 🚫 Custom study scripts 🚫

- We needed reusable pipelines, but existing tools felt heavy
  (`targets`, `glue`, etc.)
- Built `gsm::RunWorkflow()` in **April 2022**
- Migrated to **`{workr}`** for modularity and extensibility
- Now in use on **20+ studies**, qualified via
  [{qcthat}](https://github.com/Gilead-BioStats/qcthat)

::: {.notes}
Science is hard: study designs vary, metrics need tweaks, study- and
metric-level customization is required — workflows absorb that variance
without forking a script per study.
:::

## Highly standardized metric workflows

![](images/data_analysis.png)

[Analysis Workflow Vignette](https://gilead-biostats.github.io/gsm.core/pr/129/dev/articles/DataAnalysis.html)

::: {.notes}
Same 5-step shape for every KRI; only params change per metric. This is what
lets one framework cover thousands of metric runs a year.
:::

# {workr} ❤️ {pharmaverse}

Not just for ClinOps!

::: {.notes}
~8:00–18:00 — the core of this talk. The same YAML-step idea maps cleanly onto
the standard clinical data flow: RAW → SDTM → ADaM → TFL/ARD. Each stage is
"just another R package's functions, expressed as steps."
:::

## From RAW to SDTM

- `{sdtm.oak}` modularizes SDTM programming — EDC- and standards-agnostic
- Its algorithms/sub-algorithms are reusable across SDTM domains
- Goal: replicate this
  [sdtm.oak vignette](https://pharmaverse.github.io/sdtm.oak/articles/findings_domain.html)
  ![](images/sdtm_vignette.png){width=130px} using workflows

## RAW → VS: a step *is* a function call {.step1-compare}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Workflow step
```yaml
steps:
  - output: vs_raw2
    name: sdtm.oak::generate_oak_id_vars
    params:
      raw_dat: vs_raw
      pat_var: "PATNUM"
      raw_src: "vitals"
```
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
=
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
Plain R
```R
lData$vs_raw2 <-
  generate_oak_id_vars(
    raw_dat = lData$vs_raw,
    pat_var = "PATNUM",
    raw_src = "vitals"
  )
```
:::
:::

Interim object naming (`vs_raw` vs `vs_raw2`) is a deliberate choice —
preserve each step for traceability, or overwrite to save memory, exactly like
`%>%` / `|>` pipelines.

::: {.notes}
The key message: adopting a package into workr is mostly about knowing that
package, not about learning workr. One step ↔ one function call.
:::

## From SDTM to ADaM

- `{admiral}` modularizes ADaM programming, with a rich extension ecosystem
  for therapeutic-area needs
- Its docs and user guides are among the best in the R ecosystem
- Same pattern: each derivation becomes a step

## SDTM → ADaM (ADVS + MAP) {.adam-map-notes}

```yaml
steps:
  - output: advs
    name: admiral::derive_vars_merged
    params:
      dataset: SDTM_VS
      dataset_add: SDTM_DM
      new_vars: !expr exprs(TRT01A)
      by_vars: !expr exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID)
  - output: advs
    name: admiral::derive_param_map
    params:
      dataset: advs
      by_vars: !expr exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01A, VISIT, VISITNUM)
      sysbp_code: 'SYSBP'
      diabp_code: 'DIABP'
      get_unit_expr: !expr rlang::expr(.data[["VSORRESU"]])
```

- `derive_param_map()` derives mean arterial pressure from SYSBP/DIABP
- `!expr` lets steps carry quasiquotation (`exprs()`, `!!`) into params —
  a natural area for future {admiral} + {workr} collaboration

## From ADaM to TFL

- Visualization/reporting is where teams diverge the most
- One approach: a workflow step that renders parameterized R Markdown
  templates (here `gtsummary` + `safetyCharts`)
- Where to host the output (Shiny, static site, PDF over email) stays with
  the user

## ADaM → TFL: render a template as a step {.step1-compare}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```yaml
steps:
  - output: lParams
    name: list
    params:
      'dfADVS': ADVS
  - output: table1
    name: rmarkdown::render
    params:
      input: !expr here::here("report_templates", "WorkProduct1.Rmd")
      output_file: !expr here::here("TFLS", "WorkProduct1.html")
      envir: !expr new.env(parent = globalenv())
      params: lParams
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
![](images/report_picture.png)
:::
:::

Small child .Rmd templates (company standard tables/figures) stitch into a
larger "lego set" work product — pick-and-choose per delivery.

## From ADaM to ARS/ARD

- `{cards}` creates CDISC Analysis Results Data (ARD)
- Built for automation, reproducibility, reusability, and traceability

```yaml
steps:
  - output: predose_visit1_map
    name: workr::RunQuery
    params:
      df: ADVS
      strQuery: "SELECT * FROM df WHERE PARAMCD = 'MAP' AND VISIT = 'VISIT1' AND VSTPT = 'PREDOSE'"
  - output: table_predose_visit1_map
    name: cards::ard_summary
    params:
      data: predose_visit1_map
      variables:
        - AVAL
```

::: {.notes}
`RunQuery()` gives you SQL-over-data-frames as a first-class step — handy for
the filtering that usually precedes a summary.
:::

## The pattern, once, everywhere

- RAW → SDTM → ADaM → TFL/ARD: **one mental model** across the whole flow
- Integrating any package ≈ knowing that package, not learning {workr}
- Persistence is intentionally decoupled — orchestrate transforms; save to
  csv / parquet / json / a data lake as just another step

This is the slide to land the pharmaverse section on. ~18:00.

# What's new + what's next

::: {.notes}
~18:00–20:00. Everything below shipped in workr 1.1.0, after the last time we
gave this talk.
:::

## New in {workr} 1.1.0

- **Project orchestration** — phase-level config files, project/phase
  load-save hooks, optional continue-on-error, clearer diagnostics
- **Reusable load/save hooks** — incl. built-in GitHub Actions artifact
  providers to pass data between runs
- **Smarter workflow discovery** — active/inactive filtering, priority
  ordering, exact-name matching
- **Hardened automation** — GitHub, manifest, snapshot & CI coverage

::: {.notes}
Tie back to the 27k-metrics/year problem: orchestration + hooks are what make
scheduled, restartable, multi-phase runs practical.
:::

## {workr} ❤️ 🤖 — designed for agentic AI

- Breaks complex tasks into modular, inspectable steps
- Agents can **generate and execute** workflows
- {gsm} and {workr} skills coming soon
